subject: mobula ray
title: Thousands of Rays Leap Out of the Sea at Once, and Nobody Knows Why

scenes.text: Thousands of rays are jumping out of the ocean. Nobody knows why.
scenes.keywords: mobula ray jumping out of water

scenes.text: Munk's devil rays. About three feet across, and they gather off Mexico in schools of tens of thousands.
One by one they rocket straight up, clear the surface by six feet, and crash back down.
They can keep this up for hours. And they eat plankton, so it isn't about catching fish.
Scientists have three guesses: a signal to the group, a mating display, or teamwork while they feed.
Every landing is a splash you can hear across the water. Maybe the splash is the point.

description:
Munk's devil rays gather in the Sea of Cortez in schools of up to tens of thousands and leap about two metres (six feet) out of the water, one after another, for hours at a time.
They are plankton feeders about a metre across, so the jumps are not hunting. Scientists are still not sure why they do it; communication, a display to gather mates and group hunting are the leading ideas.
What do you think the jumping is for? Comment below.
first_comment: All nine mobula species jump, and so do their cousins the manta rays. Fishing nearly wiped them out of the Gulf of California in the 1980s and 90s, and they have only one pup at a time. Which ocean mystery should we cover next?
